project.name: BiteRunr
project.description: BiteRunr is an Expo/React Native mobile app for coordinating group food runs, collecting orders, scanning receipts, and settling per-line payments through Stripe Connect. The repository also includes separate admin and landing Vite apps alongside the mobile Convex backend. Note: this project has over 100 source files; consider scoping analysis to a subdirectory for faster results.

tour.title: Project Overview
tour.description: Start with the README to understand BiteRunr as a mobile-first app for coordinating group food runs, receipt scanning, and per-line settlement. It also frames the repository boundary: the Expo app and Convex backend are primary, while admin and landing are sibling Vite apps with their own deployments.

tour.title: Expo Runtime
tour.description: The Expo config defines the native app identity, plugins, permissions, React Compiler setting, and public Convex and Stripe values. The root layout then turns that configuration into a running app shell by mounting Stripe, Convex Better Auth, theme, safe-area, font, toast, and splash-screen providers before Expo Router renders screens.
tour.languageLesson: Expo Router uses layout files as React components that wrap route groups, so runtime concerns such as providers and redirects live next to the navigation tree.

tour.title: Mobile Auth Flow
tour.description: Building on the root shell, the auth and protected layouts split the app into sign-in screens and authenticated screens. The mobile auth client wires Better Auth to Convex, email OTP, and Expo SecureStore, while the auth context exposes readiness and session helpers without bouncing returning users back to loading UI during later refetches.
tour.languageLesson: React context is useful here because auth readiness and session state are cross-cutting concerns consumed by many screens without prop drilling.

tour.title: Backend Auth Bridge
tour.description: The Convex backend has its own Better Auth component, but BiteRunr's app data uses a separate users table. These files explain that boundary: Convex mounts Better Auth and push notifications, configures providers and OTP email delivery, exposes HTTP routes, and bridges Better Auth users to app users by email.

tour.title: Data Model
tour.description: Once authentication is clear, the Convex schema defines the durable entities the rest of the app talks about: users, orders, locations, items, invites, Stripe accounts, payments, squads, friends, and waitlist entries. This is the vocabulary that connects route screens, domain functions, receipt parsing, and settlement flows.
tour.languageLesson: Convex schemas combine runtime validation with generated TypeScript bindings, which keeps client calls and backend functions aligned around the same table and argument shapes.

tour.title: Main Tabs
tour.description: The protected tab screens are the user's main dashboard after login. Home aggregates orders, friends, invites, and settlements; groups focuses on active and past runs plus join flows; account gathers profile, payment state, statistics, settings, and sign-out behavior.

tour.title: Order Screens
tour.description: The order route group is where the core product workflow becomes concrete. A runner creates an order, participants add items manually or by voice, the active order screen manages participants and sharing, and the summary screen coordinates grouping, scan state, manual pricing, and the handoff into settlement.

tour.title: Order Backend
tour.description: The matching Convex functions own the server side of that workflow. Orders handles lifecycle and assembled views, orderItems manages item writes and AI-assisted grouping, and orderInvites powers QR-style invite codes with validation, expiration, usage limits, and joining.

tour.title: Receipt Intelligence
tour.description: After orders have items, receipt scanning turns a photographed receipt into owed amounts. The backend parses receipt images with an LLM, while shared grouping and fuzzy matching utilities normalize similar item names and map parsed receipt lines back to participant order lines.
tour.languageLesson: The fuzzy matching helpers combine edit-distance similarity with word-overlap boosts, a common TypeScript pattern for keeping heuristic matching deterministic and testable.

tour.title: Settlement Payments
tour.description: The settlement screens split the experience between runners tracking who has paid and buyers paying their own balance. On the backend, payment records, Stripe Connect actions, and a centralized fee helper keep card payments, in-person settlements, payouts, and platform fees consistent.

tour.title: Design System
tour.description: Most newer mobile screens build on the BR component barrel and theme tokens rather than raw styles. The generated token file and synchronization script also show how the older NativeWind CSS variables stay available to JavaScript consumers such as navigation theming.
tour.languageLesson: A barrel file such as components/br/index.ts creates a stable import surface, letting screens depend on the design system API instead of individual component file paths.

tour.title: Sibling Web Apps
tour.description: The repository also carries two web packages that are intentionally separate from the mobile app. The admin app currently hosts policy-oriented pages, while the landing app composes marketing sections and a Convex-backed waitlist form with its own deployment notes.

tour.title: Build And Checks
tour.description: End the tour with the files that explain how changes are validated and packaged outside local development. The GitHub Actions workflow runs the repository check command on pushes and pull requests, while the admin and landing Dockerfiles show how the sibling web apps become deployable services.
tour.languageLesson: CI YAML separates triggers, jobs, and ordered steps; Docker multi-stage builds separate dependency-heavy build stages from smaller runtime images.
